articles.text: Gen. Grant's condition is very serious and although there has been no definite report to that effect, there seems to be little doubt that that he is suffering from a cancer or some malignant affection of almost as serious a nature. Not till after his death will the true nobility of his grand character be appreciated.
articles.summary: Editorial note on Gen. Grant's serious illness, believed to be cancer.

articles.text: Probably the sickest lot of sore-head political tricksters that were ever congregated together, can now be found in Bismarck. The capital removal bill passed both houses of the legislature, but there was "one wide ribber to cross" before it became a law. The Governor had to affix his signature, and right here is where the combination was broken. He vetoed the bill and gave as a reason for his veto such legal reasons as are absolutely unanswerable. Wisely passing by the manifest facts that the removal bill was originated by Pierre town-site boomers and supported only by this mercenary spirit and one of revenge, the Governor confined his reasons to the legal side of the question and conclusively proved that the seat of government could never be legally changed as long as Dakota remains a territory. Governor Pierce seems to have a happy faculty of doing exactly as he pleases and always doing right. Not a trace of political corruption has fastened to him, and although he has had to decide many vexed questions, over which there had been bitter wrangling, the unanimous verdict of the people has been that he has decided them all in a perfectly unprejudiced manner,
articles.summary: Editorial applauding Governor Pierce for vetoing the capital removal bill, calling its backers Pierre town-site boomers.

articles.text: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. articles.text: Reports from all sections of the country both east and west show that this has been an exceptionally hard winter on stock. Cattle and horses, especially the former, are looking very hard. Feed has been plenty but the unusual fall of snow has made it hard to get at. It is not expected that there will be any overwhelming losses, but a larger percentage than for several years past will be the result of the hard winter. The Bad Lands will suffer with the rest, but not as severely, as the fall of snow has been less here than in less favored localities. Chinooks have only visited us two or three times this winter and but once have been of sufficient duration to entirely uncover the grass. Some of the beginners in stock business are feeling a little blue over the prospects, but old timers say that "lightning seldom strikes twice in the same place" and are confident that next year will fully recover the losses of this year. There must be some exceptions to the general rule, therefore a hard winter must be looked for occasionally.
articles.summary: Range report: an exceptionally hard winter on stock everywhere; the Bad Lands suffered less, with few chinooks, and old timers expect recovery.

articles.text: It is doubtful if any cattle will be driven from Texas this season. The railroads will not run the risk of damages from contagion, and Kansas and Nebraska have both adopted quarantine laws that are prohibitary as far as Texans are concerned. It is to be hoped that Texas fever will be investigated immediately and a cure discovered, if found to be as represented. The virtual loss of a market will be borne with difficulty by Texas cattle growers and it may be that this market is lost without reasonable cause. The best thing for the Texans to do is to have a thorough and expert examination of the source and effect of the disease and published the facts to the world. Their simple statement that there is no danger in Texas fever will now go for nothing until they prove it.
articles.summary: Range editorial: quarantine laws in Kansas and Nebraska and railroad fears of Texas fever will probably stop cattle drives from Texas this season.

articles.text: "Many are watching with great interest the steady onward march of those noble bovines of color. I believe the Missouri gentleman was correct when he said, 'The black cattle will take the country as the black hogs have.' Fifteen years ago black hogs were being introduced into Kansas and now no other kind has hardly been seen for more than five years. The progress of the cattle must necessarily be much slower, they not being so prolific as the hog. Let us stop with cattle. I rejoice to see the black muleys adorned with the many blue ribbons which they have been receiving of late and which they so well deserve. The sweeptakes prize won at the Kansas City fat stock shows last November by the Aberdeen-Angus heifer (Bride) for best dressed carcass, and the sweepstakes prizes won recenty at the World,s Fair at New Orleans by the three-year-old Golloway steer, when we consider their competitors, was a grand victory for the muleys. Happier, more contented, independent, devil-may-care sort of beings never lived. Twenty degrees below zero don't freeze them. They take on fat as readily as the slow and easy fat and greasy happy-go-lucky sort of people who laugh and grow fat. No one ever saw a black muley look sad; not even when he was being separated from his kin folks to be taken miles away never to see them again. Being without weapons, nothing fears him. Judging others as harmless as himself, he fears nothing. Further I would say that the black muley is the most cheerful, substantial, good-natured, contented, companionable bovine that your correspondent has ever had the fortune to form an acquaintance with, and i would rather feed one of them than a thousand long-horns.
articles.summary: Quoted letter praising black polled ("muley") Aberdeen-Angus and Galloway cattle and their recent prize-winning at Kansas City and New Orleans.

articles.headline: Communication.
articles.text:
The following is an account of the adventures of Jones & Pennell's outfit, written by Uncle John Seaton, whom all will remember as the one who always put up the jobs on the boys for which Bob and Joe always had to stand the blame:


Sec. 8, Croton Aqueduct, Yonkers N. Y.

A. T. Packard.

Dear Sir.

Permit me to give you a short history of our wanderings and doings since leaving Medora, the queen city of the Bad Lands. Leaving about the 16th of July last in company with your well-known friend Joe Pennell Esq. to join his partner who had taken a contract on the Canadian Pacific on the north shore of Lake Superior. This we completed on the 21st day of Dec. last, giving entire satisfaction to the company and gaining considerable notoriety as rail road builders. After remaining in camp some weeks to settle our business affairs we on January 13, received a telegram from Mr. T. G. Jones to move our forces immediately to this point where he had taken a contract of three miles of tunnel work. On leaving our camp in Ontario we fitted up six sleds to haul our baggage, blankets some rations for ourselves and forage for our mules, making comparatively a very light load, particularly our baggage which consisted of what wearing apparel we had on our persons. We anticipated rather a tedious though pleasant trip. However after encountering the snow a few hours, which measured four feet in depth, the thermometer ranging from forty to sixty below zero, atmosphere damp and heavy, we were induced to change our notions of pleasantness and felt somewhat disappointed. Anxious however to return to a "land of milk and honey" we pressed forward and accomplished our undertaking without a murmur from one of the fourteen persons composing our company. Three pairs of heavy wool mitts, four pairs of stockings of like character with Arctic overshoes, moccasins or shoepads. Even with that protection, our hands and feet suffered some from cold. Our sojourn in Ontario hardened our cheeks to such an extent that I am happy to say none were touched the slightest with frost. A few days out convinced us of the impossibility of proceeding further with our sleds, which we were reluctantly compelled to abandon at Pic River, one of the tributaries of Lake Superior, having yet one hundred miles to go before reaching rail road transportion. We had but a limited time to perform the journey, the train making only weekly trips and in the event of our missing it would compel us to remain over a week. We lighted up and packed our mules with our blankets, a small amount of rations for ourselves and some forage for the animals. Mounted on the hurricane deck of a hungry mule, we set out to cross a portion of the lake a distance of about forty miles, with quite a depth of snow on the ice and a very imperfect trail. In the afternoon we missed a certain point steered for, losing our way. We continued travelling until some time after dark, when we discovered the outlines of timbers, which proved to be a small island and afforded us good shelter. Here we made rather a comfortable camp for the night the mercury indicating about 46 below. At daylight the next morning we were again on the trail, fighting snow on an M. T. stomach arriving at our point of shipment about 1 o'clock P. M. We made an attack on the dinner table at the hotel groaning under the luxuries of Ontario, i. e. dried apples, condensed milk and oat meal porrage, which we devoured in a ravenous manner, much to the chagrin of the host and hostess. Shipping our stock to Medora and ourselves to this point, we arrived on the 14th inst., where we found Mr Jones busily engaged with a large force of men and first-class machinery, boring into the bowels of the earth to reach the top of the intended tunnel below, a distance of about fifty-seven feet through a solid rock, classed by engineers as gneiss, about like the ordinary lime stone in the west. The tunnel in length is twenty-eight miles, with twenty-six shafts, in depth of from forty to four hundred and seventy feet to top of tunnel, excavation sixteen by sixteen feet, to be bricked and cemented, for the purpose of conveying fresh water from Croton river to N. Y. city. Forty million dollars have been appropriated for the work, but it is thought a much larger amount will be requested before completion. Near our work is located one of the largest carpet factories in the country, turning out daily three miles or five thousand two hundred and eighty yards of carpet, and employing twenty-two hundred young ladies, in age from fifteen to thirty years. They are now on a strike for higher wages. As many of your ranch men and cow boys are leading bachelor lives in the far west it is suggested by Mr. T. G. Jones to follow the example of Gov. Andrews of Massachusetts, who, many years ago shipped a cargo of young ladies to California, and they were successfully married off to good husbands, many who in after years became wealthy and distinguished men. Should this experiment be carried out Mr. Joe Pennell who is so well and favorably known in the west, will be appointed Gen'l. Superintendant for the east and will be ably assisted by Mr. Howard Eaton with headquarters at Medora, who will receive them on their arrival and see that they are well cared for and properly distributed. No better appointments could be made and we feel assured that they have few superiors in handling a "calico brigade". We will watch the movements of things here, and report progress.

Yours & c.

J. P. S.
articles.summary: Letter from Uncle John Seaton (J. P. S.) at Yonkers, N. Y., recounting Jones & Pennell's outfit finishing Canadian Pacific work, a brutal winter trek, and their new Croton Aqueduct tunnel contract.

articles.headline: Dakota Legislature.
articles.text:
BILLS INTRODUCED IN THE COUNCIL.

By Mr. Richardson, amending section 7, chapter 63, laws of 1881. By Mr. Wagner, a memorial to congress placing Gen. Grant on the retired list. By Mr. Natwick, vacating certain portions of Mathews & Coburg's addition to the city of Brookings. By Mr. Pettigrew, repealing sections 64, 65, 66, 67 and 68, chapter 112, session laws of 1883. By Mr. Westover, establishing an independent school district in Woonsocket, Sanborn county. By Mr. Bowdle, providing for funding the indebtedness of the city of Mitchell; also, vacating certain blocks in Marion Junction. By Mr. Walsh, authorizing a special election in Steele county. By Mr. Jones, establishing Independent School District No. 1, Hutchinson county. By Mr. Wagner, authorizing the commissioners of Bon Homme county to fund indebtedness. By Mr. Bowdle, authorizing the commissioners of Davison county to fund indebtedness. By Mr. Walsh, vacating certain town plats and additions.

Council bills passed: Reviving and amending the charter of the city of Bismarck; vacating certain portions of Cooper's addition, city of Grafton; defining the boundaries of the county of McLean; amending section 4 of the act providing for the construction of a court house in Walsh county; improving the public school system of the city of Pierce; amending the charter of the city of Castleton.

House bills passed: Locating the seat of Sanborn county at Woonsocket; funding the indebtedness of the town of Plankinton, Aurora county; amending the charter of Vermillion.

The house spent the greater portion of the afternoon in committee of the whole considering the insurance bill recently passed by the council. Further consideration of the same is a special order for 3 o'clock to-morrow. Among the bills introduced to-day, is one by Mr. Larson relating to changes of boundaries of counties. The bill provides that the boundary lines of counties that have been organized for three or more years shall not be changed unless by a majority vote of the legal voters in the county from which the territory shall be taken. If this measure becomes a law it will doubtless do much to prevent repetitions of the county troubles that have occurred in the past.

THE SPINK COUNTY MATTER

will probably come up to-morrow in the house for discussion. Miller's bill locating the county seat at Ashton has been reported back from the committee with recommendations to pass, a minority report being submitted naming Redfield as the county seat. Both parties claim to be able to carry the day. It is quite probable that capital removal in some form will come up again this week. But ten days of the session remain, and the removers feel that if anything is to be done action must be taken soon.

Bills introduced in the house: By Mr. Larson, authorizing a charter for Elk Point. By Mr. McCall, amending sec. 32, chap. 28, political code, entitled "revenue." By Mr. McHugh, amending chap. 99, Gen. Laws of 1883, relating to the levy and collection of taxes on railroad companies. By Mr. Blakemore, providing for the publication of laws in the newspapers of the territory: also chartering the village of Woonsocket. By Mr. Myron, repealing the law providing for the appointment of superintendent of public instruction for the territory. By Mr. Williams, making county orders receivable for taxes in Burleigh county and interest bearing after presentation. By Mr. Huntington, to promote the construction of the Sioux Falls, Fairbank & Western railroad. By Mr. Dewoody, legalizing the acts of the trustees of Ipswich. By Mr. Stewart, authorizing the commissioners preventing changes in the boundary lines of organized counties; also, providing for the return of patients from hospitals for the insane to their homes. By Mr. McHugh, authorizing the commissioners of Cavalier county to fund indebtedness. By Mr. Smith, establishing a territorial horticultural and forestry association. By Mr. Swanton, establishing an independent school district in Oak Hollow, Hutchinson county; also vacating certain portions of the city of Mandan. By Mr. Williams, protecting game in Burleigh county.
articles.summary: Territorial legislature report: bills introduced and passed in council and house, a county-boundary bill, and the Spink county seat fight.

articles.text:
Bismarck, Dak., Special Telegram, March 3.—That the threats uttered occasionally during the past six weeks, by southern members in the heat of debate, that the north had not yet heard the last of the capital removal were intended to be carried out, was proven to-day by the resurrection from the special house committee of the bill relocating the capital at Pierre. The committee who have had charge of the bill for several weeks, last consisted of Messrs. Southwick, Huntington, Miller, Mark Ward and Williams. The first three gentlemen reported the bill back, recommending that it pass with the amendment that the capital should not be removed from Bismarck to Pierre until the 1st of May, 1885. Messrs. Ward and Williams submitted a minority report unfavorable to the bill. A motion was at once made to adopt the report, this being followed by another to indefinitely postpone further consideration of the bill, and this in turn by a motion to lay the motion to indefinitely postpone on the table. A call of the house was then ordered, and the last motion carried by a vote of 25 to 23. Of the southern members, Messrs. Clark, Huntington, Johnson, Huston, Langen, Dewoody and Mark Ward, voted in the negative. No sooner had the vote been announced than a bombshell was fired into the ranks of the South Dakotians in the form of a resolution offered by Mark Ward, charging W. S. Wells and V. P. Prentice of Pierre with

MAKING CORRUPT OFFERS

to members, and paying them money to vote for the capital removal bill. The resolution The council went into executive session at 3 o'clock to-day, and confirmed the nomination of Speaker Rice as attorney general. The opposition did not number more than half a dozen votes, and is said to have come from the north. Gov. Pierce's motion in nominating Rice appears to have been to select a man upon whom the south had united, and judging from the fact that Rice secured their support for the speakership, the appointment was made on that ground. The only criticism that is heard on the appointment is as to Rice's qualifications for the position. The council concurred to-day in the house amendments to the appropriation bills, with the exception of the Brookings Agricultural college, in which case a committee of conference was appointed.

Bills introduced in the council:

By Mr. Gamble, amending the charter of the city of Yankton; also, fixing the term of the district court of the Sixth judicial district. By Mr. Duncan, regulating the sale of intoxicating liquors, (providing that the commissioners of any county, upon a petition of the majority of legal voters of the county, shall refuse to grant license for the sale of intoxicating liquors. By Mr. Nickeus, annexing certain townships to McHenry county.

Council bills passed:

Changing the name of certain churches in Bon Homme county; amending sec. 5, chap. 5, Political Code; vacating certain portions of Matthew's addition to the city of Brookings; providing for the assessment and taxation of telegraph property in the territory; regulating the per diem and mileage of directors, trustees and regents of territorial institutions; offering a reward for the discovery of anthracite coal in the territory; authorizing the commissioners of Cass county to fund an indebtedness and finishing and furnishing the court house; amending certain sections of the penal code.

House bills passed:

Appropriating $5,000 for the running expenses of the normal school at Spearfish; establishing Independent School District No. 1, Douglas county.

Bills introduced in the house:

By Mr. Ward, funding the outstanding indebtedness of Marion school district, Turner county. By Mr. Barnes, prohibiting the manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquors, and providing conditions for local options. By Mr. Huston, establishing an independent school district in Harrison, Douglas county. By Mr. Morgan, exempting from assessment or taxation all lands taken for public highways. By Huston, providing for the formation of school districts. By Mr. Swanton, vacating Cherry street, town of Menno, Hutchinson county; also, providing for the relief of labor, material and men who did work and furnished materials for the capitol building. By Mr. Oliver, amending the charter of Lisbon. By Mr. Rice, establishing an independent school district in Flandreau, Moody county. By Mr. Hutchinson, authorizing the commissioners of

Nelson county to fund indebtedness. By Mr. Williams, authorizing the city of Bismarck to issue $15,000 of bonds to pay for sewerage.

The committee appointed by the house today to investigate the charges of bribery, met in the parlors of the Sheridan House this evening and organized for work. Some preliminary evidence was taken. Prentice was called before the committee and denied the charges, claiming ability to prove his innocence. Prentice and Wells will appear before the committee to-morrow, at 10 o'clock, with an attorney to conduct their cases. The names of Dewoody and Pierce, members of the house, have been mentioned in connection with the case. Rich developments may be looked for to-morrow.
articles.summary: Bismarck dispatch of March 3: the capital-removal-to-Pierre bill is revived 25 to 23, Mark Ward charges W. S. Wells and V. P. Prentice with bribery, Speaker Rice is confirmed attorney general.

articles.text:
As an offset to Mark Ward's bribery resolution introduced recently into the house, the opposite party introduced another in the council, through Westover, which reads as follows:

Resolved, That a committee of five be appointed by the chair to investigate charges of corruption and attempted corruption of members of this legislative assembly, and the offer of bribes by Alex McKenzie, A. W. Edwards, L. G. Johnson and W. F. Steele, for the purpose of influencing votes upon the question of the removal of the capitol, now pending before the legislature, and that said committee be instructed to proceed at the earliest possible moment to take action in regard to such charges and to procure witnesses and take testimony.

and that they report their action and findings with all convenient speed.

After presenting the resolution Westover spoke excitedly for some ten minutes, claiming that definite knowledge had come to him that the gentlemen named had made corrupt offers to certain members, and that the same could be proved. Nickeus objected to the insertion of Steele's name, as that gentleman is a member of the house, and that one house had no right to investigate the action of a member of the other. Pettigrew spoke for several minutes in support of the motion, taking the ground that the council had a perfect right to call Steele as a private citizen before its committee. The motion passed, and Westover, Gamble, Lamoure, Twomey and Farmer were appointed a committee of investigation.

IN THE HOUSE

this morning the northern members made an attempt at delay on capital removal by moving that the clerk be ordered not to transmit the bill passed yesterday until ordered by a majority vote of the house. This called out hot words from the friends of the bill, and for nearly an hour the usual wrangle occurred, but the motion was finally lost, by a vote 25 to 23, the same as that of yesterday on final passage; consequently the bill was transmitted to the council this afternoon, where it was given a second and third reading and referred to the special committee who have had charge of a similar council bill for the past six weeks.

After disposing of the capital removal bill, the house settled down to business and passed a large number of bills, among which were Smedley's railroad bill, Gamble's bill providing for the organization of new counties, and Washabaugh's bill calling a constitutional convention at Sioux Falls in September.

These bills will doubtless receive the governor's approval. The railroad bill calls for the appointment of three commissioners, one each from North, Central and South Dakota. It is generally conceded that the Central Dakota appointment will be tendered Col. Smeadly, who is the father of the bill and well informed on the subject of transportation. The name of Alex Griggs of Grand Forks has been prominently mentioned as the candidate of North Dakota, while in the south there are several candidates for the office. The council committee on election reported Pickler's woman suffrage bill back to-day, with an amendment submitting the question to a vote of the people at a general election next November, recommending the bill to pass as amended.

BILLS INTRODUCED IN THE COUNCIL.

By Mr. Smeadley, providing for county auditors in the counties of Brown, Day, Grant, Coddington, Deuel and Sargent; creating a joint school township in Griggs and Steele counties; authorizing the commissioners of Benson county to fund indebtedness; providing a charter for the village of Northwood, Grand Forks county.

Council bills passed:

Authorizing the formation of county mutual insurance companies; establishing an independent school district in Woonsocket.

The council passed house bills, providing for the funding of the indebtedness of the following counties: Ramsey, Sargeant, Union, Edmunds, Aurora and Dickey; relating to pine lands in Minnesota; creating a territorial department of agriculture; regulating county fairs, and providing for the report of agricultural societies.

Bills introduced in the house:

By Mr. Rugar, legalizing school township election in Township No. 2, Turner county; by Mr. Blakemore, amending the charter of the city of Huron; by Mr. Barnes, amending sec. 1, chap. 48, Laws of 1879; by Mr. Hobart, amending secs. 58 and 59, chap. 21, political code; by Mr. Oliver, keeping county offices open from 9 a. m. to 12 m., and from 2 to 5 p. m., each day; by Mr. Martin, amending chap. 10, political code; by Mr. Smith, repealing chap. 37, special laws of 1883; by Mr. Griggs, legalizing assessment in Butte county; by Mr. Coe, deepening the boundaries of Oliver and Mercer counties; by Mr. Barnes, amending sec. 54[illegible], Civil Code; by Mr. Hobart, amending sec. 12, chap. 62, Special Laws of 1881; by Mr. Pickler, fixing the salaries of district clerks at $200 per annum in counties having population of less than 5,000, $300 in counties having more than 5,000; also, amending sec. 658, chap. 4, Civil Code.

HOUSE BILLS PASSED.

Funding the indebtedness of Fort Ransom school township, Ransom county; amending the act incorporating the city of Chamberlain; creating Washington county and defining its boundaries; enabling the voters of Lamoure county to vote upon the location of the county seat; for the relief of Milton C. Conners; ascertaining the acreage of timber in the territory; amending sec. 79, chap. 28, Political Code; amending the act incorporating the village of Parker, Turner county; changing the name of Logan, Aurora county; dividing Emmons county and creating Winona county; incorporating Big Stone city.

Council bills passed:

The substitute bill providing for the appointment of railroad commissioners; amending sec. 553, code of criminal procedure; reimbursing Brown county for money paid out in taking care of certain paupers; providing for the organization of new counties; providing for a constitutional convention and formation of the state constitution, preparatory to the admission of Dakota into the Union; amending sec. 237, code of civil procedure; extending the boundaries of the city of Grafton; authorizing the commissioners of Turner county to fund indebtedness; amending sections 25 and 26, article 2, city charter of Jamestown; authorizing School District No. 78, Walsh county, to issue bonds to fund indebtedness; amending chapters 52 and

53, laws of 1883; incorporating the city of Milbank.
articles.summary: Westover's counter-resolution in the council to investigate alleged bribes by Alex McKenzie and others; the house sends the capital bill to the council; railroad commission, new counties and constitutional convention bills pass.

articles.text:
After some debate, the bill recently passed by the house, locating the Central university and appropriating $15,000 for the construction of the same at Ordway, was passed by a vote of 12 to 11.

Kennedy's pet scheme. The debate on this bill was opened by Smedley, Kennedy's colleague, who claimed that Central Dakota was justly entitled to the university, on account of her position and population. Kennedy also spoke for several minutes in support of the bill, indulging to some extent in personalities. After some further debate the roll was called and the bill passed by a vote of 12 to 11, Cameron not voting. All the northern members but Walsh voted in the affirmative, and all the southern members but Bowdle, Kennedy, Smedley, Wagoner, and Westover in the negative. This matter disposed of,

THE CAPITAL BILL

was next put upon its third reading. It has been conceded by the north for some time past that the bill would pass the council, the only question being by what majority. Nickeus, determined to furnish some amusement and perhaps worry the south a little, moved to amend by striking out the words "Pierre, Hughes county," and inserting "Stone Falls, Minnehaha county." This caused laughter at Pettigrew's expense. After the amendment was voted down Nickeus moved to insert Brookings in place of Pierre. This motion at once brought Natwick to his feet, who, taking the matter in earnest, stoutly protested that Brookings did not want the capital. This amendment was also voted down. The south then began to suspect that Nickeus meant to amend by moving to insert the name of the town of each southern member in turn, and the spectators were also of the same opinion. To preclude the possibility of any such procedure, Pettigrew jumped to his feet and moved the previous question which was carried. The bill was then put on its final passage and carried by a vote of 14 to 10.

Affirmative—Cameron, Dray, Duncan, Farmer, Gamble, Huetson, Jones, Kennedy, Natwick, Pettigrew, Smedley, Washabough, Wells, Westover.

Against—Austin, Bowdle, Flittie, La Moure, McLaughlin, Nickeus, Richardson, Twomey, Wagner, Walsh.

The fact that but forty-one of the seventy-two members of the legislature voted for its passage is strong argument in favor of the supposition that an executive veto will be attached. Gov. Pierce has also put himself upon record by depreciating any further agitation of the former troubles on the ground that such action would be inimical

to the best interests of the territory. The south places great emphasis on the fact that, as amended, the bill provides the removal shall not take place until May 18, 1886, claiming that removal at that late date will do much to secure division, an object dear to every South Dakotian's heart. On the other hand, the northern men claim, and with apparent good reason, that the territory cannot break the contract entered into with Bismarck, whose citizens have proceeded in good faith throughout. Great excitement prevails, but citizens of Bismarck do not feel greatly alarmed as yet at the prospect of losing the capital. After the disposal of the capital question, the council took up Pickler's woman suffrage bill, recently passed by the house and reported back from the committee yesterday with an amendment that the question be submitted to a vote of the people at the general election in November. Some discussion occurred on the bill, and an amendment inserting November 1886 instead of 1885 was lost by a vote of 13 to 11; Pickler meantime rushing hither and thither on the floor in the endeavor to secure support for his measure. It soon became evident, however, that the friends of the bill were

IN THE MINORITY.

Nickeus was their chief champion, while Gamble led the opposing forces, most of the other members remaining silent. On the roll call the bill was carried by a vote of 19 to 5, the only members voting in the nega-

tive being Gamble, La Moure, McLaughlin, Washabaugh and Walsh. Several who voted in the affirmative did so in the belief that woman suffrage would be snowed under by a large majority if submitted to a vote of the people. There are but ten members of the council really in favor of extending the ballot to woman. This vote practically kills the bill, as when sent to the house the amendment will not be concurred in. The council did but little else during the afternoon of importance. The house spent the day in committee of the whole on general orders. Among the measures considered was the bill locating the county seat of Spink county at Ashton, recommended to pass by a vote of 30 to 8. Bills introduced in the council:

By Mr. Walsh, establishing Independent School District No. 2, in Grand Forks county. By Mr. Natwick, defining the boundaries of the Fifth judicial district and fixing the time of holding court therein. By Mr. Nickeus, authorizing the judges of district courts to change judicial subdivisions and create subdivisions. By Mr. Washabaugh, supplementary to chap. 28, Political Code.

Council Bills Passed—Authorizing the city council of Mitchell to fund indebtedness; vacating certain blocks in the town of Marion Junction, Turner county; vacating certain town sites in Bon Homme county.
articles.summary: The council passes the Central university (Ordway) bill 12 to 11 and the capital removal bill to Pierre 14 to 10, effective May 18, 1886; Pickler's woman suffrage bill is amended to a popular vote.

articles.text:
The governor returned the bill appropriating $35,000 to the Fargo Agricultural college and $8,000 for the erection of a reform school building at Plankington with a veto message.

The message was well received and, upon roll call, sustained by a unanimous vote as to the Fargo agricultural college, one councilman voting to pass the Plankinton bill over the veto.

The bill removing the United States Court from Yankton to Mitchell came up in the house, passed by a vote of 28 to 12 but was killed in the council. The bill locating the county seat at Ashton passed the house by a vote of 33 to 12 and will pass the council.

COUNCIL BILLS PASSED.

Creating a joint school township in Griggs and Steele counties; authorizing Bon Homme county to fund indebtedness; annexing certain unassigned townships to McHenry county; creating Miner county a judicial subdivision of the Second district court, to be held the first Tuesday in May; defining the boundaries of the Fifth judicial district; fixing terms of court in the Sixth judicial district; providing for taxing railroads on gross earnings, with amendments renewing the present law as to taxation of lands; creating Ransom and Turner counties a subdivision of the Third judicial district; authorizing the directors of the Sioux Falls penitentiary to lease the United States a wing of the penitentiary.

House bills passed:

Extending the term of the county auditor of Pembina and other counties; establishing a highway along the county line between Yankton and Turner counties; for securing public health against unwholesome provisions; amending the charter of the city of Larimore; memorializing congress to improve the water way between Big Stone lake and the Red river; amending the act of 1883, relating to highway labor; defining the boundaries of Ransom and Benson counties; authorizing the village of Egan to issue $20,000 of bonds; making Nelson county a subdivision of the Third judicial district.

Bills introduced in the house:

By Mr. Williams, changing the name of the town of Victoria, McLean county, to Coal Harbor. By Mr. Morgan, making an appropriation for the construction of a sewer for the capitol building. By Mr. Steele, amending the special laws of 1883. By Mr. Runkle, incorporating the city of Salem, in Cook county. By Mr. Johnson, creating Adams county. By Mr. Pickler, regulating the receiving and transportation of fuel on railroads. By Mr. Oliver, changing the name of the town of Marshall to Enghoah. By Mr. Rice, amending the charter of Flandreau. By Mr. Huntington, appropriating funds to pay for steam heating in capitol building. By Mr. Williams, establishing an independent school district in Walcott, Richland county; also, changing the name of Walter James to Walter Cushing. By Mr. Eldridge, providing for bonding the indebtedness of the Big Stone school township.

House bills passed:

Establishing a territorial normal school at Groton; providing for the organization and government of the university of the Missouri; amending sec. 12, code of civil procedure; changing the name of the village of Nordland, Kingsbury county, to Arlington; establishing a fence law in the counties of Fall River, Custer, Pennington, Lawrence and Butte; amending sec. 15, justices' code, creating a subdivision of the Sixth judicial district; regulating the term of office of county treasurer in the counties of Cass, Grand Forks and Traill; providing for transcribing records in Edmunds and McPherson counties; relating to the foreclosure of chattel mortgages; providing for the erection of a court house and jail in Clark county; incorporating the village of Aberdeen; creating Adams county; amending sec. 17, chap. 28, political code.

Council bills passed:

Authorizing Stutsman county to issue bonds to fund road and bridge indebtedness; authorizing the commissioners of Codington county to fund indebtedness; authorizing the commissioners of Cass county to issue bonds for finishing and furnishing the court house, and for funding the road and bridge debt; amending sec. 656, civil code; authorizing Walsh county to build a court house.
articles.summary: Governor vetoes the Fargo Agricultural college and Plankinton reform school appropriations; the bill moving the U. S. court from Yankton to Mitchell dies; long lists of bills passed.

BILLS INTRODUCED IN THE COUNCIL.

By Jones, defining powers of the Presbytery of South Dakota. By Bowdle, amending the city charter of Chamberlain.

House bills passed:

Providing for the erection of a court house in Clark county; incorporating the city of Clark; relating to county seat of Spink county; changing the name of Nordway village to Arlington; amending the code of civil procedure relative to appeals by counties; making Burleigh county warrants receivable for county taxes; amending the penal code so that penitentiary sentences may be less than one year; creating a county of Adams; providing for annual elections in Faulk county to locate the county seat until it is located on a railroad; creating the office of commissioner of immigration; for the issue of McPherson county funding bonds; revising and amending the civil code relative to insurance companies; for the protection of prairie chickens, plover and other game; authorizing Minnehaha, Miner, Kingsbury, Beadle, Sully and Aurora counties to aid persons whose crops were destroyed by storms; prohibiting civil officers from entering into contracts with municipalities or the territory.

Bills introduced in the house:

By Mr. Larson, amending section 1 and repealing section 6 of the act relating to bonds and coupons issued by township of Elk Point. By Mr. Parshall, providing for the purchase of 100 copies of the first and second volumes, Dakota reports. By Mr. Huntinton, authorizing Andover school township, No. 9, Day county, to issue bonds to build school houses. By Mr. Steele, amending the charter of the city of Steele. By Mr. Williams, establishing a commission on legislation.

HOUSE BILLS PASSED.

Incorporating the city of Salem, McCook county; amending the act establishing Independent School District No. 1, Turner county; establishing Independent School District No. 2, Turner county; amending the charter of the city of Lisbon, Ransom county; appropriating $1,500 to defray the expenses of the territorial board of agriculture; appropriating $260 for the construction of a sewer and cesspool for the capitol building; supplementary to art. 4, chap. 11, Code of Civil Procedure; amending sec. 2, chap. 77, General Laws of 1881; amending chap. 10, Political Code, providing that a term of the supreme court be held once each year at each of the following cities: Bismarck, Yankton and Deadwood; relating to foreclosure of mortgages on real estate to be foreclosed in court rather than by advertising; amending sec. 672, political code; relating to certificates; amending secs. 58 and 59, chap. 21, political code; amending sec. 32, chap. 28, political code, providing that the governor, treasurer and auditor constitute a board to levy a proportionate territorial tax; authorizing the commissioners of Roberts county to fund indebtedness; incorporating the village of Woonsocket; establishing an independent school district in Flandreau, Moody county; amending the charter of the city of Steele; amending sec. 1 and repealing sec. 6, laws of 1881, relating to bonds of Elk Point; defining the boundaries of Kidder county.

Council bills passed:

Establishing territorial and county boards of health; providing for the organization and maintenance of territorial militia, and appropriating $15,000 for their support.
articles.summary: The council takes up the $392,700 omnibus appropriation bill for territorial institutions; the immigration commissioner bill and other measures pass.

articles.text: By recent action of the legislature Parker is now the county seat of Turner county. The records were removed from Old Swan Lake and placed in a two-story frame building at the head of Main street.

articles.text: W. H. Merrifield, of Ferris & Merrifield, went east this morning to Minnesota and Iowa to buy a herd of cattle to be added to the Maltese cross outfit. He will return about the first of May.
articles.summary: W. H. Merrifield of Ferris & Merrifield went east to buy cattle for the Maltese Cross outfit.

articles.text: Two car loads of pipe and fittings have arrived and the boilers are expected daily. An assistant engineer will soon arrive from Winnipeg, who will take charge of the tanking, which will all be done at night.
articles.summary: Pipe and fittings arrived for tanking work; boilers expected.

articles.text: The slaughter-house will be finished in about three weeks. Owing to the change in the plans, the roof will be raised four feet. Peter Book has the contract for the smoke stack, which will be eighty five feet high, with a twenty foot base.
articles.summary: The slaughter-house nears completion; Peter Book to build an 85-foot smoke stack.

articles.text: Tuesday morning there was an arrival at the Metropolitan who departed from the usual rule and did not register. The arrival was a young lady and weighed eleven pounds. Mrs. Fitzgerald is the happy mother.
articles.summary: A daughter weighing eleven pounds was born to Mrs. Fitzgerald at the Metropolitan.

articles.text: There must have been a large gorge down the river as the water raised nearly five feet night before last. It came up to the foundations of the new slaughter house and Dan Williams had to almost swim back after going out to see what the trouble was.
articles.summary: An ice gorge sent the river up nearly five feet, reaching the new slaughter house.

articles.text: J. W. Gallup came in on yesterday's coach from Cave Hills to get his papers made out as post master at that place. The post-office department has advertised for bids for carrying the mails from Medora to Deadwood, the contract to begin July 1.
articles.summary: J. W. Gallup came from Cave Hills to qualify as postmaster; bids advertised for the Medora-Deadwood mail.

articles.text: The roller rink will be open Tuesday. Thursday and Saturday evenings from eight to half-past ten. Tuesday and Thursday afternoons from three to five the rink will be open to ladies and children exclusively. Saturday afternoons the rink will be open to all. Competent instructors will be on hand to assist beginners.
articles.summary: Roller rink hours announced.

articles.text: George Wilkes captured a large bat last night at the slaughter house that is a curiosity. It is much larger than ordinary, is of a reddish color streaked with white and belongs to a very rare species. It is rather long in the body and is very heavy for its size. George will send it east for exhibition in a few days.
articles.summary: George Wilkes caught a large, rare bat at the slaughter house.

articles.text: There hasn't been a minute during working hours for five months that the sound of hammers has not been heard in Medora. Fram the present prospect it would seem that the same sound will continue all summer. Several new buildings will be put up immediately and others will come later. The best of it is that no useless ones are erected and there is pressing demand for store rooms now.
articles.summary: Five months of continuous building in Medora, with more to come.

articles.text: If Howard Eaton hadn't told us we never would have belived it, but Bob Roberts was passing as a dude in New York. He had a plug hat, gold headed cane, piccadilly collar and lah-de-dah necktie and patent leather boots. He must also have been ailing some as the report comes from the same reliable source that he went in search of a smile Sunday and got fired from a wet goods store for a spotter. Hence these tears.
articles.summary: Joke that Bob Roberts was passing as a dude in New York, per Howard Eaton.

articles.text: The opening ball of the skating rink was a complete success. About twelve sets were danced and then the skating began. The floor was pronounced very satisfactory and all enjoyed themselves to the utmost. The craze has struck Medora and every one who has not learned is going to try the "little wagons." Messrs. Fisher and Deffebach were much pleased with the attendance and a maple floor will be the next thing on the programme.
articles.summary: The skating rink's opening ball was a success; Fisher and Deffebach plan a maple floor.

articles.headline: The Bad Lands Gun Club Shoot.
articles.text:
The second shoot in the series of five for the rifle, took place last Saturday. As the score shows, there was a material improvement over the preceding shoot and doubtless still more must be made by the winner of the gun. Below will be found the score of Saturday's shoot and the present rank of the contestants:

[Score table, 100, 200 and 300 yards; individual shot scores not transcribed. Totals:] Paddock 57; Packard 55; Wyland 54; Piper 50; Book 47; Young 47; Foster 39; Chute 38; Hannigan 35; Williamson 34; O'Sullivan 33; Brown 33; Fisher 33; Van Driesche 29; Jorgens 28; Cook 16 at 100 yards, 0 at 200, "Scattered." at 300.

TOTAL SCORE FOR TWO SHOOTS. (Rank, 1st, 2nd, Total)

Paddock 1, 55, 57, 112

Packard 2, 52, 55, 107

Piper 2, 57, 50, 107

Wyland 4, 52, 54, 106

Book 5, 45, 47, 92

Chute 6, 49, 38, 87

Williamson 7, 38, 34, 72

VanDriesche 8, 39, 29, 68

Foster 9, 28, 39, 67

O'Sullivan 10, 29, 33, 62

Jorgens 11, 30, 28, 58

Brown 12, 23, 33, 56

Fisher 13, 20, 33, 53

Hannigan 14, 13, 35, 48

SHOOTLETS.

It's a cold day when any one misses the butte.

Next Saturday's contest will begin promptly at 1:30,

The six-eyed blonde didn't make allowance for the wind Saturday.

Fisher may think his mountain howitzer will carry two hundred yards but no one else does.

The contestants must be more prompt in shooting. It was too dark before the close last Saturday.

Messrs O'Hannigan and McSullivan were overheard concocting a scheme to [pool?] their scores and "yank the sassige."

Captain Paddock has change of all points coming up that do not need the ttenention of the executive committee.

Cole & Bicknell make good markers but resigned when they thought Fisher was turning loose on them with his Gatling gun.

It seemed to be the prevailing opinion that the two eyes the blonde drove on the lead sort o' jack-knifed on him at two hundred yards.

The gun rack and the rules prohibiting contestants from handling the guns or loading before stepping to the scratch are great improvements and materially lessen the danger of accidents.

Last Sunday Brown was digging bullets out of the butte back of the target but seemed to lose all interests in his occupation when Joe O'Brien began turning loose at it. It was a narrow escape and all should be careful about going behind the target as some one is liable to fire at it any time.
articles.summary: Scores of the second of five Bad Lands Gun Club rifle shoots; Paddock leads, Packard and Piper tie for second; joking "Shootlets."

articles.text: There are several principles to be observed in new towns which must be followed out if the town is to be a success. Chief among these principles is the one of "help your neighbor." It is a very easy thing and a very short-sighted thing to say, "we are not here for our health," and then send out of town for what you want instead of patronizing home industries, or perhaps start an opposition to one already established because there seems to be a little money in it and the idea never occurs to these men that where there is a living for one there will be starvation for two. But, some one will say, we can get our own goods cheaper in this way. Let us see if you can. A successful town is one where plenty of money is in free circulation. The mere fact that it passes rapidly from hand to hand is enough to guarantee the success of the town. Every one is satisfied because every one has money. On the other hand, take the extreme case of a town where every one buys where he can buy the cheapest. Nine times out of ten, especially in a small frontier town, this must be at some large town in the east. In this case then, all the circulating medium that we spoke of in the former illustration as going to make a successful town is sent away and the consequence is inevitable. The town is as dead as a horse-thief at a Montana neck-tie social. This illustration of all the money being sent out of town is, of course an extreme one, but it serves to establish the principle which serves to make a successful place. Looking at the matter in this light, is it not perfectly manifest that it is more profitable to spend your money at home? Of course you pay more for the articles you buy, but you get correspondingly higher wages if you are a laboring man or more for your goods if you are a merchant. This principle we have illustrated is scarcely a greater factor in the success of a town than the principles of avoiding over-production and ruinous competition. Because one man makes money out of manufacturing an article it is no sign that two will. It is a very easy thing to glut the market in a small town and then the dealers are sure to lose. In any event, competition in a small town so divides the trade that neither of the competitors make any money. Take our own town as an illustration. There is not a business man in it who is not satisfied and making money. But there is not an established business here that can stand the division of trade that will inevitably follow competition. We have made these remarks, not because our people as a class are guilty of them, but because a few are and others may be mis-led into being guilty. "Let him, whom the shoe fits, wear it."
articles.summary: Editorial urging Medora people to buy at home and avoid ruinous competition that would divide a small town's trade.
